objective.n: Sentence 2 needs a contrast ("however"); "although" from the box is used as the nearest choice.

shortQuestions: Jahangir Khan was a weak and sickly child and had hernia operations, so doctors advised him to avoid physical activity. But squash was in his blood — his father Roshan Khan and brother Torsam were champions — and he had a strong will to play and succeed, so he ignored the advice and kept practising.

He followed a very hard training routine: long runs (about nine miles a day), sprints, rope skipping, weight training and yoga, hours of court practice every day, a disciplined diet and early sleep — all under the guidance of his father and cousin Rehmat Khan.

He won the World Amateur Championship at fifteen, became the youngest World Open champion at seventeen (1981), won the World Open six times and the British Open a record ten times in a row (1982–1991), and remained unbeaten for over five years (about 555 matches) — one of the longest winning streaks in sport.

Jansher Khan, another Pakistani squash legend, also won the World Open a record eight times and dominated squash in the 1990s. Like Jahangir he showed great fitness and determination, but Jahangir is remembered for his unbeaten run of five years, while Jansher is known for the most World Open titles. (Students may compare any national sports hero.)

Examples: 'to have something in one's blood' — to inherit a talent or interest from family; 'to rise to the occasion' — to perform well when needed; 'to make history' — to do something important that will be remembered. (Any three idioms from the text with correct meanings.)

His life teaches that weakness can be overcome by determination, hard work and discipline; that respect for elders and guidance, humility in victory and self-belief lead to greatness; and that a person can bring honour to his country through dedication.
activities: Sample essay — The Present State of Squash in Pakistan: Pakistan once ruled the world of squash — Hashim Khan, Roshan Khan, Jahangir Khan and Jansher Khan won the British and World Opens for decades. Today, however, Pakistan has no player in the world's top rankings. Reasons include lack of modern facilities and coaching, few courts outside a few cities, poor sponsorship, the security situation that stopped international events, and the popularity of cricket. To revive squash, the government and federation should build courts in schools, hire foreign coaches, organise junior tournaments and give scholarships to young talent. With proper planning Pakistan can regain its lost glory.

Group sharing guide: students who like the same game sit together and each gives reasons — e.g., cricket: teamwork and national popularity; squash: fitness and speed; football: global appeal; hockey: our national game — then one member reports the group's main reasons to the class.
